skills.title: Signs & squares
skills.tagline: Keep the sign with the number.

lesson.explanation: A negative times a negative is positive. Squaring a negative number means multiplying that whole number by itself. Brackets matter.
steps: In (−4)², both factors are −4, so the product is +16.
In −4², square 4 first, then apply the minus sign.
Keep the brackets when substituting a negative coefficient.

skills.title: Read the coefficients
skills.tagline: Find a, b and c, including their signs.

lesson.explanation: Put the equation in the order ax² + bx + c = 0. The numbers attached to x² and x are a and b. The constant is c.
steps: A missing x term has coefficient 0.
The coefficient of x² is 1 when no number is written.
The sign immediately before a term belongs to its coefficient.

skills.title: Substitute a value
skills.tagline: Replace every x with the same number.

lesson.explanation: To test a value, replace every x with that value. Work out powers, then multiplication, then addition and subtraction.
steps: Put brackets around the value you substitute.
Calculate x² before multiplying it by its coefficient.
If the final value is zero, the number is a root of p(x) = 0.

skills.title: Find the factor pair
skills.tagline: Two numbers, one sum, one product.

lesson.explanation: To split the middle term of ax² + bx + c, find two numbers with sum b and product a × c. For a monic quadratic, a is 1.
steps: List factor pairs of a × c.
Choose signs so the product is right.
Check the sum as well. Both conditions must work.

skills.title: The zero-product rule
skills.tagline: A zero product needs a zero factor.

lesson.explanation: If A × B = 0, at least one factor must be zero. Set each factor equal to zero separately. You do not need both factors to be zero at once.
steps: A product can be zero because the first factor is zero.
It can also be zero because the second factor is zero.
This shortcut applies to a product equal to zero, not a sum or a nonzero product.

skills.title: Solve a linear factor
skills.tagline: Undo one operation at a time.

lesson.explanation: Keep both sides equal. Add or subtract the same amount on each side, then divide by the coefficient of x.
steps: Add 3 to both sides.
Divide both sides by 2.

skills.title: Square roots & fractions
skills.tagline: Keep the whole numerator over the denominator.

lesson.explanation: The square-root symbol means the non-negative square root. The ± sign gives two branches. Divide the whole numerator by the denominator.
steps: Find the square root first: √16 = 4.
Calculate the plus and minus branches separately.
When a root is not an integer, keep it exact as a surd, or use the stated decimal accuracy.

lesson.explanation: A quadratic equation has highest power 2 after you expand, collect terms and move everything to one side. Its standard form is ax² + bx + c = 0, with a ≠ 0.
steps: Expand both sides: x² + x + 8 = x² − 4.
Subtract x² from both sides. The square terms cancel.
The remaining equation is linear. Seeing x² at the start is not enough.

skills.title: Meet the roots
skills.tagline: Find the values that make it true.

lesson.explanation: A root is a value of x that makes the equation true. For standard form, substitute the value and check whether the left side equals zero.
steps: Replace every x with 1.
The left side is 2 − 3 + 1 = 0, so 1 is a root.
A quadratic has at most two distinct real roots. A repeated root has just one distinct value.

skills.title: Factor it out
skills.tagline: Turn one quadratic into two smaller equations.

lesson.explanation: Rewrite the quadratic as a product of two linear factors. Then use the zero-product rule to solve each factor separately.
steps: Find numbers with product 2 × 3 = 6 and sum −5: −2 and −3.
Split and group: 2x² − 2x − 3x + 3 = 2x(x − 1) − 3(x − 1).
Factor: (2x − 3)(x − 1) = 0. Set each factor to zero: x = 3/2 or x = 1.

skills.title: Use the formula
skills.tagline: A method even when factors are hard to spot.

lesson.explanation: Identify a, b and c, keeping their signs. Compute D = b² − 4ac. If D is non-negative, the quadratic formula gives the real roots.
steps: x = (4 ± √8)/2 = 2 ± √2. The entire numerator is divided by 2a.

skills.title: Read the discriminant
skills.tagline: Know the kind of roots before solving.

lesson.explanation: The discriminant is D = b² − 4ac. Its sign tells you how many distinct real roots the quadratic has.
lesson.example: D>0:\ 2\text{ distinct}\qquad D=0:\ 1\text{ repeated}\qquad D<0:\ 0\text{ real}
steps: Positive: two different real roots. They need not be integers.
Zero: two equal roots, or one distinct repeated value.
Negative: no real roots. This chapter works with real numbers.

skills.title: Make it real
skills.tagline: Turn a situation into an equation.

lesson.explanation: Define what x means. Translate the relationship into an equation, solve it, then check which roots make sense in the situation.
steps: The equation is 2x² + x − 300 = 0.
A width cannot be negative. The width is 12 m and the length is 25 m.
